note.overview: The model considers the intraday scheduling problem in a group of orthopaedic clinics where the planner schedules appointment times, given a sequence of appointments. The model considers patient re-entry—where patients may be required to go for an x-ray examination, returning to the same doctor they have seen—and variability in patient behaviours such as walk-ins, earliness, and no-shows, which leads to inefficiency such as long patient waiting time and physician overtime. In our data set, 25% of the patients are required to go for x-ray examination.

source.quote: Problem definition: We consider the intraday scheduling problem in a group of orthopaedic clinics where the planner schedules appointment times, given a sequence of appointments.

We consider patient re-entry—where patients may be required to go for an x-ray examination, returning to the same doctor they have seen—and variability in patient behaviours such as walk-ins, earliness, and no-shows, which leads to inefficiency such as long patient waiting time and physician overtime.

We consider patient re-entry—where patients may be required to go for an x-ray examination, returning to the same doctor they have seen—and variability in patient behaviours such as walk-ins, earliness, and no-shows, which leads to inefficiency such as long patient waiting time and physician overtime.
Results: Our model achieves significant reductions, in comparative studies against a sample average approximation (SAA) model, on patient waiting times, while keeping server overtime constant.
These are tabulated in Tables 6–9 in Online Appendix B, summarizing the performance metrics of our model against the two benchmarks.
Our simulations further characterize the types of uncertainties under which SAA performs poorly.
